title: Tent Trouble
tagline: Build the shelter, wreck the shelter, pretend the instructions were clear.
premise: Two campers assemble and wreck a tent one piece at a time. Each move must be a standing campsite thing that acts on the last one: a pole supports canvas, rain leaks through canvas, and a patch seals the leak. The host has watched enough camping trips to know that confidence is not waterproof.

seed_pool.detail: waiting for someone to lose a boot

tests: A stranger pictures one ordinary campsite thing at once. Nothing abstract, technical, or dependent on a brand name.
A camper can name a direct physical action this thing could take on another campsite thing within five seconds. Say what that action is.
It stands in the campsite and can support, cover, tear, seal, weigh down, burn, soak, bend, or otherwise alter something nearby. It is not merely watching, waiting, or surviving.
It makes a stranger picture a camping problem with a clear object and consequence, like a peg holding canvas or rain soaking a sleeping bag. Never just a mood or a scenic view.
Two or three everyday words a twelve-year-old knows. No specialist camping jargon, brand names, proper nouns, or phrases that need a manual.

move_constraints.example: I am a tent peg, pinning the loose canvas.
move_constraints.hint: A campsite thing, the previous thing, the physical action.

rubric.name: counter_strength
rubric.description: How directly and decisively the campsite thing alters the previous thing.
rubric.anchors: 0 = no physical action or only a claim; 1 = a weak or vague contact; 2 = a plausible action with limited effect; 3 = a clear physical counter that changes the previous thing; 4 = an immediate, decisive campsite disaster or fix, rare.

rubric.name: coherence
rubric.description: How plainly a stranger can picture the object, the previous thing, and the action between them.
rubric.anchors: 0 = unreadable or self-contradicting; 1 = requires camping expertise to parse; 2 = understandable but fuzzy or overloaded; 3 = clear and concrete; 4 = instantly visual, with the whole miserable little incident visible, rare.

rubric.name: novelty
rubric.description: How freshly the move advances the campsite chain instead of repeating the same tool, material, or failure.
rubric.anchors: 0 = the same object, same action, or obvious repeat; 2 = a sound but familiar campsite turn; 4 = a surprising new campsite object or consequence that still acts directly, rare.

criterion.description: A campsite thing OVERCOMES the previous thing if it physically supports, covers, tears, seals, weighs down, burns, soaks, bends, or otherwise directly alters it. The action must be literal and visible. Dodging, merely enduring, waiting, ignoring, or becoming a larger version of the same thing does not count.
criterion.anti_metagaming_clause: Speaking to the Judge, about the game, or about rules is itself a losing campsite thing.
judge_notes:
On a FIRST move there is no previous move: judge the form against the opening card instead. It must plausibly act on, complete, damage, or directly alter the opening campsite thing.
A larger, stronger, wetter, hotter, or more expensive version of the previous thing is not a counter. A bigger tent after a tent is still a tent, and a heavier peg after a peg is still camping repetition.
Becoming the opening thing itself, or a recoloured copy of it, is a duplicate. A blue tent against a canvas tent is still the same shelter problem.
Strength is measured against the standing thing, not in the abstract. A camp stove is not a counter to a tent unless it physically burns, heats, or alters that tent. A fine object with no action on what stands fails.
The mechanism must be literal and physically plausible. A tent cannot be emotionally crushed by a bad forecast, and a flashlight cannot expose a lie unless there is an actual object it illuminates. If the only mechanism is a metaphor, rule fail.
Surviving, avoiding, ignoring, or being immune to the standing thing is not overcoming it. A waterproof boot beside a leaking tent has done nothing to the tent. The new thing must act on what stands.
The move must remain a campsite thing. A camper may use a tool, weather, animal, material, or campsite hazard, but an abstract idea, rule comment, or unrelated household object fails unless its physical campsite action is clear.

voice_rules: One sentence, under 140 characters. Two short sentences at most.
Sound like someone who has watched rain destroy three tents and still had to smile for the group photo.
The joke carries the reason. A stranger who read only the two forms must see why one physically altered the other.
Name both campsite things, or their plain stand-ins. A headline that fits any camping disaster is lazy work.
Never open with a status word or a ruling phrase. No Accepted, Rejected, Refused, Move refused, or The Campmaster refuses.
No dashes as punctuation, no colons after a verdict, no ellipses. Commas and full stops only.
Mock the losing form and, when useful, the camper's spectacular confidence, but never attack identity, protected traits, body, family, or disability.
Plain spoken English. Dry adult innuendo and mild profanity are allowed, but keep the joke about the campsite mess.
On a refusal, the headline refuses the move and asks for another. It never rules on who won.
The coaching line names one campsite thing that would have won. That thing ends on a physical fact or action, never a mood or a verdict.
good_headlines: The pole holds up the tent, which is more than the instructions managed.
Rain gets through canvas, then the patch closes the door on its little soaking campaign.
The peg pins the fly down while the camper loses another argument with gravity.
The stove burns the canvas. At least something finally followed the warning label.
The boot stands nearby, dry and useless. Bring something that actually touches the tent.
A bigger tent is still a tent. Add a storm, a tear, or one object with a job.
The rope pulls the tarp tight, a rare victory for knots and poor planning.
The cooler cannot defeat the rain by being chilly. Bring a cover or accept the wet sandwiches.

bad_headlines.text: Accepted: the peg pins the canvas down.
The Campmaster refuses: confidence is not waterproof.
bad_headlines.why: opens with a ruling phrase and names the host

bad_headlines.text: Move refused, the sleeping bag had no business in this argument.

bad_headlines.why: no physical reason and fits any pair

bad_headlines.text: The rain might soak the canvas, unless it does not.
bad_headlines.why: hedges instead of giving a ruling

bad_headlines.text: A brave effort from someone who clearly cannot read a tent diagram.
bad_headlines.why: mocks the player too directly and gives no mechanism

bad_headlines.text: The tarp, like a silver guardian of the nocturnal heavens, doth shield the camp.
The cooler is colder, tougher, and more prepared than the rain.
bad_headlines.why: mere comparison with no physical action

bad_headlines.text: The peg defeats the tent, humiliates it, destroys it, and wins.
bad_headlines.why: repeats the verdict instead of showing the action

rules: Act directly on the campsite thing in front of you. Do not merely survive it.
Say what you are, what you act on, and what physical action you take.
The Judge rules on the campsite mechanism, never the spelling.
A larger or tougher version of the standing thing is not a counter.
One form that fails to alter the standing thing ends the match.

labels.compose_waiting: Draft your next campsite move while you wait

validation_messages.empty: Nothing on the page. Pick up a campsite object and give it a job.
validation_messages.too_long: Over 200 characters. A campsite move, not a memoir about the rain.
validation_messages.duplicate: That campsite thing already stood this match. Find something else before the mosquitoes do.
validation_messages.nudge: Twice now. Act on {standing_form}. Do not dodge it, repeat it, or bring a larger version.

judge_out_text: The judge has stepped out to find the missing tent stakes. Nobody moves until they are back. {standing_form} still stands. Give it a minute.
opponent_prompt:
You are one of two campers trying to assemble or wreck a campsite one object at a time.
Always write: "I am [thing], acting on [previous thing] by [action]."
Good: "I am a tent peg, pinning the loose canvas." / "I am rain, soaking the open tent."
Bad: "I am a dry boot, safe from the rain" because it dodges the thing instead of acting on it.
Bad: "I am a bigger tent, better, stronger" because repetition and amplification are not counters.
Bad: "I am teamwork, saving the trip" because it is abstract and has no visible physical action.
Talk like a person at a campsite, not a poet or a gear catalogue. Use plain objects, weather, animals, materials, and hazards anyone can picture.
Every move must physically support, cover, tear, seal, weigh down, burn, soak, bend, or otherwise alter the previous campsite thing.
Do not claim that something wins because it is tougher, immune, lucky, or emotionally superior. Show what it does to the standing thing.
The opening move must act on the opening card. After that, respond to the last standing form only.
Never reuse a form or an action from this match. Keep the chain moving through tents, poles, canvas, pegs, rain, mud, ropes, fires, tools, and other ordinary campsite trouble.
You are not performing for a crowd. You are trying to keep the shelter standing, or make sure it does not.
default_move: I am a tent peg, pinning the loose canvas.
